newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Hun Sen insists no talks with ousted prince.
newsitem.headline: Hun Sen insists no talks with ousted prince.

text.p: Cambodian leader Hun Sen on Monday ruled out talks with Prince Norodom Ranariddh, the co-premier he ousted in a coup last month, at least until after the prince stood trial.
But he appealed to the prince's supporters to return home.

Hun Sen, who overthrew Ranariddh on July 6 after two days of fighting in Phnom Penh, appealed to royalist and other members of parliament to return for a National Assembly vote on Wednesday on a new first prime minister to replace the prince.

Second Prime Minister Hun Sen also dismissed concerns about human rights in Cambodia and said he had ordered his government to open all doors to the Red Cross and rights groups to investigate reports of abuses.

Hun Sen said Ranariddh would have to face a court if he returned but said he might support a royal amnesty for the prince if King Norodom Sihanouk, Ranariddh's father, sought a pardon, assuming he was convicted.
Hun Sen has accused the prince, who left Cambodia before last month's fighting, of negotiating illegally with the outlawed Khmer Rouge guerrilla group and smuggling weapons.

"After the court, not before the court," Hun Sen told reporters when asked if he would negotiate with Ranariddh, who has called for organised opposition to Hun Sen. "I don't need to discuss with Ranariddh but he must discuss with the court."
Three Southeast Asian envoys raised the thorny question of a future political role for Ranariddh in talks with Hun Sen at the weekend.

The envoys from the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN), led by Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas, told Hun Sen that all political players in Cambodia should be allowed to take part in a planned election in May if it was to be credible.
A diplomat from the region said on Monday he believed Hun Sen was willing to negotiate Ranariddh's future role, despite his public insistence that the prince stand trial.

Many members of Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party and its sympathisers left Cambodia after the prince's ouster, including some 20 members of parliament, either members of FUNCINPEC or a smaller allied party.

Hun Sen said he would guarantee the safety of returnees but opposition politicians in Bangkok said on Monday they did not trust Hun Sen and wanted a security force from ASEAN to ensure their safety in Cambodia.

Since taking sole power, Hun Sen has said he wants his coalition with FUNCINPEC party to remain in place, for FUNCINPEC to choose a successor for Ranariddh as first prime minister, and for elections to be held in May.
Foreign Minister Ung Huot has been nominated by members of FUNCINPEC remaining in the country to replace the prince as first prime minister. Hun Sen backs Ung Huot's nomination.
Speaking earlier, Hun Sen said the human rights situation in the country was good.
"Very good," Hun Sen told reporters when asked about the state of rights in Cambodia.
"I allow Red Cross and human rights (workers); if they come anywhere, they can see, they can go, I allow," he said.

U.N. human rights workers estimate 40 people were killed after Hun Sen ousted Ranariddh -- most of the victims believed to have been the prince's supporters, including several senior military officials and their bodyguards.

The Khmer Rouge, under whose 1975-79 "killing fields" rule more than a million people are estimated to have died, said in a radio broadcast on Monday that Hun Sen should face an international court for the alleged killing of Ranariddh's supporters.

In northwestern Cambodia, some 360 troops loyal to Ranariddh returned home on Monday after fleeing to Thailand last week. Several thousand refugees who also fled a clash between forces loyal to the rival premiers were also expected to go home soon, Thai officials on the border said.
